text: Suppose you change the system prompt, swap in a newer model, or retune the weight of your hybrid search. Did the product get better? Reading five outputs and feeling encouraged is not evidence, because language models vary from one run to the next and five examples cover almost nothing. An evaluation, or eval, replaces that impression with a measurement, built from a fixed set of test cases, a grader that scores each answer, and a statistic that summarises the scores honestly.

The test cases matter most. The best ones come from your own traces, real requests that real users sent, chosen to cover the situations you care about, including the hard and the embarrassing ones. Each case records what a good answer must contain or do. Keep the set fixed while you compare versions, and keep it separate from any examples you used while tuning, or the score will flatter you.

Grade with code whenever you can: exact matches, valid JSON, a required citation, a test suite that passes. For qualities that code cannot check, a second model can act as a judge with a written rubric, but the judge must be validated first. Label a sample of answers by hand and measure how well the judge agrees with you using Cohen's kappa, which discounts the agreement two graders would reach by chance alone, the way two people flipping coins would still agree half the time.

A score from two hundred cases is an estimate, so it needs an error bar. The bootstrap provides one without any formulas. Draw two hundred cases from your test set with replacement, so that some appear twice and some not at all, recompute the score, and repeat this a few thousand times. The spread of those scores shows how much the result could move by luck, and the middle ninety five percent of them gives a confidence interval.

To compare two versions, grade both on exactly the same cases and look at the differences case by case. A paired comparison like this cancels out the variation between easy and hard questions, so it detects real improvements with far fewer cases. Bootstrap the difference in the same way, and if the interval comfortably includes zero, you have not yet shown that the new version is better.

Numbers tell you whether something changed, while reading failures tells you why. Error analysis means reading the failed cases, sorting them into categories, and fixing the largest category first. Every bug you find becomes a new test case, so the suite slowly turns into a regression test that guards against old mistakes coming back, much like the unit tests in ordinary software.

These ideas apply to any system built on a model, but agents and retrieval pipelines raise particular difficulties. An agent's answer arrives at the end of a long chain of actions, and a retrieval pipeline can fail in its search or in its writing. The final lesson of this module looks at how to evaluate them.
